title: Baron approves Fonseca: God knew conditionally what Adam would do before decreeing to permit the fall
source_text: XXVI. Robertus quoque Baronius expresse probat sententiam Fonsecae ponentis in Deo scientiam quandam conditionatam, ante liberum ipsius decretum, quae futurorum absolutam praescientiam antecedat. Deum, verbi causa, prius conditionate tantum scivisse quid eventurum esset, si Eva seducta a Serpente Adamum tentaret; postquam autem decrevit permittere ut Adamus obtemperaret uxori suae suadenti, non amplius conditionate, sed absolute praevidisse Adamum lapsurum.
pass_a_gloss: XXVI. Robert Baron also expressly approves the opinion of Fonseca positing in God a certain conditional knowledge, before his free decree, which precedes the absolute foreknowledge of futures. That God, for example, first knew only conditionally what would come to pass, if Eve seduced by the Serpent should tempt Adam; but after he decreed to permit that Adam should obey his wife persuading him, he foresaw no longer conditionally, but absolutely that Adam would fall.
pass_b_english: Robert Baron also expressly approves Fonseca's view, which posits in God a certain conditional knowledge before his free decree, preceding his absolute foreknowledge of future things.

For example, God at first knew only conditionally what would happen if Eve, led astray by the serpent, tempted Adam. Once he decreed to permit Adam to obey his wife's persuasion, he foresaw no longer conditionally but absolutely that Adam would fall.

lemmas.latin: non amplius conditionate, sed absolute praevidisse
lemmas.gloss: foresaw no longer conditionally, but absolutely

choices.why: Knowledge of what would happen under a condition; kept as the technical counterpart to middle knowledge.
